name: Manhattan
tagline: Twitter's in-house, multi-tenant, eventually consistent key-value store with pluggable storage engines.
description: Manhattan is the distributed database Twitter built in-house as a self-service, multi-tenant storage platform for its engineers; it had been in production for about two years when Twitter described it publicly in April 2014. Its core handles routing, topology, intra- and inter-datacenter replication, conflict resolution and continuous replica reconciliation; above that sit pluggable storage engines (seadb, a read-only format for batch Hadoop output; an LSM 'sstable' engine for write-heavy data; and a B-tree engine for read-heavy data) plus services for Hadoop bulk import, strong consistency (consensus with a replicated log enabling check-and-set) and high-volume time-series counters for Twitter's observability stack. It is eventually consistent by default and schemaless key-value. Manhattan was never open-sourced or sold, so it matters as a design reference rather than an option.
statusNote: Internal to Twitter/X and never released externally; its current role at X is not publicly documented.

pricing.notes: Not available outside Twitter/X; no licensing or service offering exists.

scale.notes: Multi-tenant clusters replicated within and across Twitter datacenters at Twitter scale.

strengths: Pluggable storage engines matched to batch, write-heavy and read-heavy workloads
Self-service multi-tenancy: teams provision storage without schemas or tickets
Optional strong consistency (consensus and CAS) on an eventually consistent core
Efficient serving layer for datasets generated in Hadoop
weaknesses: Not available outside Twitter/X; no source, binaries or docs
Public technical detail stops around the mid-2010s
useCases: Reference design for multi-tenant, multi-datacenter key-value platforms
Studying pluggable storage engines and replica reconciliation
notIdealFor: Anyone outside X: it cannot be obtained
